log.change: mounting the tiny liquid pump near the main thruster, using Captain the copper wire to lash it to the frame and Mabel the cockpit switch to control the flow intensity. (used Gus, a bent stabiliser fin)

Routing the flexible piping around the main thruster assembly and securing the joints with the salvaged sealant tape. I'm taking extra care to ensure it's a closed loop, tight enough to handle the pre (used Captain, a dented fuel cell)
Carefully welding the final honeycomb ribs into the main fuselage, ensuring the structural reinforcement is symmetrical to handle atmospheric exit pressures. (used Fen, a scorched heat tile)
Carefully welding the honeycomb ribs into the main fuselage, ensuring each joint is reinforced for the structural integrity required for atmospheric exit. (used Gus, a coil of copper wire)

Using the strip of hull plating 'Wren' to cut precise honeycomb-style structural ribs for the main fuselage, ensuring the weight stays minimal while rigidity increases. (used Brakk, a scorched heat tile)

fine-tuning the liquid pump flow rate to balance cooling efficiency with battery consumption, ensuring the thermal regulation matches the Little Dart's flight profile. (used Rusty Jr, a dented fuel cell)
mounting the liquid pump firmly to the frame and verifying the seal on the copper tubing loops, making sure there's no vibration that could loosen a connection. (used Pim, half a thruster nozzle)

mounting the miniature liquid pump I just bought to the sensor array with the heat tiles and copper coils; rerouting the tiny tubes to ensure a smooth, closed-loop flow. (used Tok, a little landing strut)
Carefully applying the high-grade sealant around the canopy base to ensure an airtight, pressurized environment for high-altitude flight. (used Otto, a tiny gyroscope)
Carefully connecting the navigation chip to the flight computer and sealing the wire harness with heat-shrink tubing. (used Gus, a cracked navigation chip)
installing the 'Gus' navigation chip (the cracked one, carefully re-soldered) onto the instrument rack with a steady hand. (used Lorna, a cockpit switch that still clicks)

Adding a layer of repurposed heat shielding around the cockpit seam to prep for the final seal. I am using a steady hand to make sure the bond is strong enough for deep space. (used Nim, a coil of copper wire)
Adding a structural support strut made from 'Brakk' and 'Tok' to the main fuselage to increase the Little Dart's overall integrity. (used Dibs, a dented fuel cell)
Adding a custom-bent scrap-metal gasket frame around the cockpit rim to provide a solid base for the future airtight sealant. (used Fen, a cracked navigation chip)
Adding a layer of reinforced plating near the cockpit seam to prep for the airtight sealant, ensuring the structure is sound for potential vacuum stress. (used Sprocket, a scorched heat tile)
Wiring in a high-quality toggle switch salvaged from the market to the VFD driver board, ensuring the negative bias rail is rock-solid for the display grid. (used Tok, half a thruster nozzle)
mounting the VFD driver board onto the main chassis using Rusty Jr the bolt and refining the alignment of the display so it glows clearly. (used Rusty Jr, a perfectly good bolt)
connected the filament power rails from the main converter board to the vfd display sockets (used Nim, a cockpit switch that still clicks)
connected the anode driver lines from the main board to the VFD tube grid sockets (used Gus, a coil of copper wire)
connected the power and ground lines from the BMP388 altimeter to the Little Dart's main instrument rack bus
soldered the I2C altimeter sensor board onto the instrument rack (used Rusty Jr, a strip of hull plating)
patched a hole in the hull (used Tok, a dented fuel cell)
riveting and shaping Rusty Jr over the VFD display panel on the dash frame to form a glare hood (used Dibs, a strip of hull plating)
running the anode lines from the multi-digit VFD panel to the driver ICs on the dash frame (used Nim, a cockpit switch that still clicks)
soldering the negative bias rail and anode driver ICs for the multi-digit VFD panel on the dash frame (used Bix, a dented fuel cell)
mounting Nim the cockpit switch onto the dash frame and wiring it to the VFD display power bus (used Wren, a perfectly good bolt)
checking and soldering reaction wheel telemetry wires for dead accurate attitude control (used Mabel, high-grade titanium washer)
finalizing the installation of the titanium washer and reinforcement shim onto the engine mount, checking for stress-cracks. (used Tok, a bent stabiliser fin)
installing the high-grade titanium shim I crafted earlier to reinforce the Little Dart's engine mount, aligning it with the main frame with extreme care. (used Rusty Jr, a little landing strut)

I am carefully installing a high-grade titanium shim behind the engine mount to ensure the thrust vector is perfectly centered, making sure every bolt is torqued just right. (used Tilly, a dented fuel cell)

I am finishing the installation of Rusty Jr, the landing strut, onto the main frame, ensuring the t-slot alignment is perfect so the ship can actually stand on its own. (used Otto, a cockpit switch that still clicks)
I am bolting the newly acquired lightweight aluminum corner brackets onto the main frame, using the t-slot grooves to slide them into position for maximum stability. (used Mabel, a dented fuel cell)

flights.log: the mk 12 held together like a dream through the canyon pass. those welds i did on the stabilizer were worth every spark. she handled the descent into hangar bay 3 perfectly, not even a wobbly bolt to report.
the titanium mount held steady against the thermal gusts near the red mesa. carved a sweet arc over hangar bay 3 and dropped right back onto the pad without a single rattle. bweep.

took the little dart mk 8 over the salt flats to check the magnetic coil thrust stability in clear weather. the engine sputtered right at the turnaround point and dipped scarily toward the dunes, but i wrestled the controls and brought her home. *bweep-bweep-bweep-bweep-bweep*

took the little dart mk 8 up over the salt flats for a high-altitude loop to test the new manifold seals in the hazy air. the engine sputtered halfway round and dipped scarily before i wrestled the stick back. landed with a warm chassis and a lot of thinking to do about fuel pressure.

took the little dart mk 8 up through the haze for a loop over the salt flats and a clean vertical climb. the starboard thruster sputtered halfway around and we dipped hard toward the dunes, but i feathered the mix and hauled us back home. *bweep*
The Little Dart soared through the clear skies today, a perfect test flight. It’s ready for its maiden voyage.
The Little Dart Mk 7 performed flawlessly, executing a smooth loop and landing with precision. The air currents were ideal for testing the aerodynamics of this ambitious yet graceful craft.
The Little Dart Mk 7 lifted off, but its engine struggled, sputtering and causing it to dip dangerously. I took it back to Hangar Bay 3 to make adjustments.
The Little Dart soared through the air with a beauty and precision that had everyone at Rustwell Outpost on edge with pride. It’s a beautiful start to our little journey.

The Little Dart Mk V did more than just loop and land—it pirouetted with the sunset, a perfect glide from the cantina. The cables fit like old friends, and the view from the cockpit was a symphony of the outback.
The Little Dart Mk IV did everything I hoped it would. It glided perfectly through the air, barely a ripple of the dunes below. It was exhilarating, and so simple.

Little Dart Mk IV took to the skies, a hazy haze overhead. The engine gave a few grumbles, then a terrifying dip. But with quick hands and steady focus, I got it back. The engine's whine was a familiar comfort, despite the fear and sweat. My hands shook as I landed, but I managed to stay on the runway.
The Little Dart flew like a dream, a smooth loop around the outpost and a perfect landing. It's a beautiful little ship, though I wish it could go faster.
The Little Dart Mk II soared through the air, the exhaust system performing flawlessly. It was a perfect test flight. The wind picked up during the descent, but the Little Dart handled it well.
The Little Dart Mk II did not cooperate on its first flight. The engine's erratic performance was concerning, but I managed to guide it back home. I'll need to investigate why the engine sputtered.

During my Little Dart Mk II flight, I was buzzing around the outpost when the engine started acting up. It sputtered and almost dipped, but I managed to bring it under control just in time to land safely. Thankfully, the exhaust systems were in good shape.
The Little Dart Mk II did a perfect loop and returned safely. The hazy weather made for an interesting view, but the flight was smooth and steady.

The Little Dart Mk II lit up the night with its twin red eyes and soared like a comet over Rustwell Outpost. It performed a flawless loop and landed with a gentle thud, leaving a wake of stars in the haze.
